column1: # Leave-out robustness for every significant cell in the Figure 3 battery.
# Test: drop the top 10% of each set's genes by |log2FC| in that cell type, refit
#   the permutation test. Proportional, so small and large sets are treated alike.
#   Result: 6 of 20 cells survive (30%).
# HOW TO READ THAT NUMBER - two calibrations, and only one of them licenses a claim.
# POWER (the relevant one). 81 sets built with GENUINE signal - true shifted genes
#   spiked into a random background at three doses - that reached P<0.05 were put
#   through the same trim. Only 16 (20%) survived. So the trim removes most real
#   signals too: it has LOW POWER, and failing it is weakly informative.
#   The battery's 6 of 20 (30%) is statistically indistinguishable from that
#   true-signal rate (Fisher OR 1.74, P = 0.37).
# SPECIFICITY (reported for completeness, does NOT license the above). 35 random
#   null sets that reached P<0.05 by chance survived at 2 of 35 (6%). This measures
#   how often the trim clears a set with no signal, not how often it clears a real
#   one, and the difference from true-signal sets is not significant (P = 0.09).
# P-MATCHED, because chance-significant sets cluster at the 0.05 boundary while
#   battery cells reach 0.001. Survival by starting-p bin:
#     start p        null      true-signal     battery
#   Bin counts are small; treat these as descriptive.
# CONCLUSION: the trim cannot be used to classify individual cells as true or
# false. Passing it is reassuring; failing it says the cell depends on its
# largest-effect genes, which is true of most real signals at this effect size.
# Report the caveat per cell, do not use the 14-of-20 count as a verdict.
